I am 67 years old. I have farmed the same land in Quzhou County since I was a young man, and my father taught me everything I know. I never went to school, but I know this soil and this climate. I do not need a book to tell me what grows here.

I have 5 mu of land. That is enough for a man my age to manage, especially since my sons are working in Shijiazhuang and I am mostly on my own. I do not try new fancy crops. Every year I plant wheat in October and maize in June after the wheat comes off. This is the way it has always been done on the North China Plain, and I see no reason to change.

My wheat is already in the ground — I sowed it last autumn after the rains, around October 10th. I used an improved local variety, the kind we call "shimai" around here. It is reliable. I tilled the land with my rotary tiller before sowing, broadcast the seed at about 30 jin per mu, and gave it a winter irrigation so it would survive the cold. Now that spring has come, I will topdress it with urea when the weather warms, and irrigate three more times before harvest in early June. I also spray for weeds once, and for insects and disease two or three times — the aphids and powdery mildew always come. I expect about 1000 jin per mu if the weather treats me fairly.

The day after I harvest the wheat in June, I will plant maize. There is no time to waste — the growing season is short. I will use a hybrid seed, probably Denghai 605 or Nongda 372. I trust these seeds; they have good drought tolerance and give me a decent yield. I will not till the soil — there is no need. I will plant directly into the wheat stubble, put down compound fertilizer at sowing, irrigate twice during the summer, and spray for pests three times. If all goes well, I will get about 1200 jin per mu by late September or early October.

I keep some grain for my own food and for feeding, and I sell the rest. The money is not much, but it is honest work, and at my age I prefer to stick with what I know rather than gamble on something new.
